‘Not a time for panic’: Governor says Missouri is prepared for possible lead fallout from Iowa blast
State officials expect minimal health risks but are preparing to monitor drinking water, farmland and livestock as the Army’s planned detonation is cleared to proceed by a federal appeals court.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe speaks to reporters on May 27, 2025 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Gov. Mike Kehoe sought Monday to reassure Missourians concerned about possible lead contamination from a planned military detonation in southeast Iowa, saying state agencies are preparing to monitor drinking water, farmland and public health but expect little risk to the state.
“This is not a time for panic,” Kehoe said during a briefing at the state Capitol. “We do not anticipate significant impacts, but we will not allow Missouri to be unprepared.”
The U.S. Army has planned to detonate about 9,700 pounds of deteriorating lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, roughly 57 miles north of Missouri. The explosive material has become increasingly unstable, military officials say, and could detonate unexpectedly if temperatures fall.
Kehoe said Missouri does not control when the operation takes place and shares neighboring states’ frustration over how federal officials have handled it.
Although his administration has held calls with the White House, Army, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and other federal officials, he said the state still has limited information.
“Based on the information we do have, we anticipate minimal impacts to Missouri,” he said.
The most specific preparations involve drinking water.
Trump says he ordered Army to cancel lead azide detonation in Iowa unless court agrees
Department of Natural Resources Director Jake Buxton said 10 Missouri drinking water systems, with 13 water intakes, are within 100 miles of the ammunition plant.
The EPA is collecting samples of untreated surface water from systems within that radius before the detonation and plans to test untreated and treated water afterward. Missouri officials have contacted the 10 systems and sent sampling supplies to regional offices to prepare for additional testing.
Buxton said the state also has been in touch with water systems in Hannibal and Louisiana, both of which draw from the Mississippi River. Earlier projections suggested any potential contamination would reach the river north of Missouri, he said, and the department did not expect the lead to affect those cities’ water intakes.
He emphasized that surface-water drinking systems already have treatment processes capable of removing lead and could adjust their operations if testing showed a need.
The extent of any fallout will depend heavily on weather conditions. Public Safety Director Mark James said a National Weather Service meteorologist and a National Guard civil support team are helping state officials model potential particle movement.
State health officials likewise do not expect a public health emergency.
Department of Health and Senior Services Director Sarah Wilson said projected lead exposure in Missouri is low and the event is expected to be brief. Her agency will continue tracking dispersion forecasts and exposure levels, she said, and anyone worried about possible contact with lead dust should consult a local health department or medical provider.

For what seemed like an incredibly long time, the women’s race at any ultra got far less attention than the men’s race. The Western States 100 — with its historic, record-setting performances by Ann Trason, Ellie Greenwood, Courtney Dauwalter, and this year, Jenn Lichter — was perhaps ahead of the rest when it came to recognizing the incredible performances by women.
It’s fitting, then, that “Raise the Bar,” a film by Hilary Yang and Carrie Highman, uses the 2025 Western States 100 as its backdrop to tell the story of four women runners — three elite and one non-elite — as they train and compete in the event. And there’s one thing that’s incredibly clear throughout the film: Women’s racing is where it is today because of the audacious, strong women who came before.
The four athletes in the film are nothing if not diverse in their backgrounds, running styles, and personalities. China’s Fu-Zhao Xiang returns after coming in second in 2024 and running the third-fastest time in the race’s history. Heather Jackson, a successful triathlete for 15 years who turned to trail running and gravel cycling, is chasing another top-10 spot after her seventh-place finish in 2024. Eszter Csillag, a Hungarian living in Hong Kong, is a mom of two young kids. She’s been third place at the race twice. Cindy Shepard of Portland, Oregon, a non-elite runner coached and mentored by ultrarunning legend Yassine Diboun, adds a refreshing dose of reality to a film genre almost exclusively obsessed with elites and the front of the pack. Her story reminds us that we do this largely for the love of the community and adventure, and not the pursuit of podiums.
History of Women in the Western States 100
At nearly 90 minutes, “Raise the Bar” has room to breathe. Not only does the film cover the current state of women at this iconic race, but it also does an excellent job of telling the robust and rich history of the Western States 100, a foot race founded in 1977 by “The Gang of Four,” including two women: Mo Livermore and Shannon Weil. The historic footage of the early years of the race offers a perspective on the oldest ultra in the U.S.
That history sets the stage for the women who spent the next several decades pushing the sport forward, a lineage brought to life in the film by voices like Dauwalter, Magda Boulet, Meghan Canfield, and Greenwood. You cannot talk about the women’s bar being raised without the name Trason, who set a course record that stood untouched for 18 years and came in second overall behind the legendary Tim Twietmeyer in both 1994 and 1995. Then Greenwood broke that record in 2012. Eleven years later, in 2023, Dauwalter didn’t just break it; she shattered it by over 90 minutes.
The women’s field in the 2025 race didn’t have any of the returning champions, leaving the race wide open with no clear favorites, but calling it anything but an incredibly competitive field would be incorrect. “There is this aura in the entirety of the women’s field where those things that you could view as untouchable are actually achievable,” says Jason Koop, coach of both Xiang and Csillag, of the 2025 women’s field. Generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race. You might only get a few chances per year to run a marathon, but you can stack up multiple half marathons, 5Ks, and 10Ks per season, as long as you balance those harder efforts with sufficient recovery time.
But jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results. Even if you feel ready to race again soon after a half marathon, specifically, you might need more time than you think. So what’s the ideal reset time after 13.1 and when should you be able to line up again?
Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.
Evaluate Your Effort, Distance, and Race Goals to Set Your Recovery Time
In general, it’s a good idea to take two to four weeks off from high-intensity work after a half marathon before racing again, says Laura Norris, a Seattle-based certified personal trainer and run coach with a master’s in applied exercise science.
You should first take three to five days postrace off completely to clear up any muscle damage and let your body fully recover, then stick exclusively to easy running for the rest of that two- to four-week period.
“There’s new research that shows the half marathon stresses the heart pretty decently for two weeks postrace,” Norris says. While it’s not the same level of stress as a full marathon, it’s still important to take sufficient time to recover before tackling another high-intensity effort.
With that in mind, you can make adjustments to your timeline:
If you raced well and feel well…
The harder you push, the longer it takes to recover, so Norris suggests waiting those three to four weeks before racing again if you just ran your fastest half marathon, even if you feel good.
However, you can consider your upcoming race distance and goal: If you’re jumping into a Turkey Trot 5K for fun, for example, you can probably get away with just two weeks of recovery, but wait at least the entire four weeks before gearing up for a full marathon, Norris suggests.
If you raced well but feel bad…
After a race where you feel really beat up, you’re extra sore, mentally drained, or fatigued, it’s a good idea to take those first three to five days off followed by two to four weeks of really easy running, Norris says. But that doesn’t mean you jump right into another race.
In this case, “it might be worth spacing your races at least six to eight weeks apart, maybe even a full training season apart,” she says. Otherwise, you could enter into a vicious cycle of overtraining, not recovering fully, and entering another race underprepared and beating yourself up again, Norris explains.
If you raced poorly but feel well…
It can feel really disappointing to train hard for months for your race and not have results to reflect that work, but it’s important to honor your recovery and health more than performance.

President Donald Trump said on Saturday, Nov. 21, that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, the Associated Press reported. “I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot,” he told Fox News Channel’s “Saturday in America.”
The obvious targets are card issuers like JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Capital One (COF). But the stock with more to lose is Upstart Holdings (UPST), which earns nearly all of its fees from unsecured lending, led by personal loans it pitches as a way to pay off credit cards. (SoFi Technologies (SOFI) has a smaller version of the same problem.)
A 10% cap finally has a path
Trump first called for a 10% cap in January, but the Republican-controlled Congress did little with it. Democrats take control of both the House and the Senate in January, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who’s expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee, has said many times that she wants to cap rates. The median card rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve, so a capped card would charge less than half that.

Upstart’s business runs on card debt
Unsecured lending brought in $929.2 million of Upstart’s $950.0 million of fees in 2025, according to its annual report. Upstart’s sample loan is $10,000 over five years at a 19.12% interest rate plus an 8.31% origination fee, for a 23.48% APR.

Today’s big story: Reported SEC Probe: Could Nvidia Stock Fall To $92?
Update, Nov 23: Large tech stocks rose in Monday morning trading after Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Amazon rose about 4%, to about $256, and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) rose about 7%, while Anthropic was about flat. The figures below are at Friday’s close.
Amazon.com (AMZN) closed at $246.82 on Friday, Nov 20. That was a fall of 4.1% for the day. Anthropic (ANT), newly listed, fell 8.5% on its second day of trading. Why mention both? This article looks at how much of Amazon’s profit came from gains on stocks and stakes it holds, and what a slide like Anthropic’s could mean for that profit.
The answer is a large share. Over the four quarters to September 2026, 40.1% of Amazon’s pre-tax income was non-operating income. That is profit from outside the business itself, such as gains on stocks and stakes a company owns. Almost all of it was gains on securities, $69.7 billion.
That is new for Amazon. From 2019 to 2022, non-operating items were a small net loss, -6.0% of pre-tax income. From 2023 to September 2025, they were 9.3% of pre-tax income. So Amazon’s reported profit now rises and falls with the prices of what it holds. The income statements do not show which holdings produced the gains. So we do not size any single one, Anthropic included.
Which Quarter Brought In Most Of The Gains?
Most of it came in one quarter. In the three months to June 2026, Amazon’s non-operating income was $53.4 billion. That was 66.0% of its pre-tax income. It was also the largest of any quarter since the start of 2019.
Net income that quarter was $62.6 billion. Operating income, the profit from selling goods and services, was $27.5 billion. So net income was 2.3 times operating income.
Amazon’s net income in the three months to June was 2.3 times its operating income. If Amazon is a big part of your savings, the profit it reports can drop fast when the stocks it holds fall. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.
Net income also ran 1.4 times operating cash flow that quarter. Operating cash flow is the cash the business brings in from customers after its running costs.
Did The Gains Keep Coming After June?
No. In the three months to September, Amazon had a non-operating loss of $1.2 billion. Gains on securities became a loss of $0.7 billion. Operating income that quarter was $28.1 billion.
Even with those swings, cash kept pace with profit over the year so far. In the first nine months of 2026, Amazon’s net income was $113.6 billion. Its operating cash flow was $113.8 billion. Profit and cash about matched.
That cuts against the idea that Amazon’s profit ran far ahead of its cash. Over the four quarters to September, net income was 0.8 times operating cash flow. The gains made the profit figure jump. They did not leave it short of cash.

Business activity declined to a six-month low in November, with manufacturing performing worse than the services sector, according to the S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index published on Monday.
The French private sector is at its most pessimistic about the coming year since late 2012, excluding the months at the start of the pandemic, according to the survey, with job losses recorded for a seventh straight month.
Among the biggest challenges cited by companies were economic conditions, uncertainty, competition and cost pressures, while frail domestic demand is weighing on sales.
France is heading toward a closely watched presidential election in April 2027, with polling suggesting voters may favor candidates offering a break from the policies associated with incumbent President Emmanuel Macron.
Politico polling this year has consistently indicated the front-runner is far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who has recently made efforts to appease financial market jitters over France's fiscal sustainability, but has failed to convince many analysts that she can stabilize the country's debt trajectory.
The latest PMI figures add to a run of economic woes for France this year, including a dramatic rise in government borrowing costs, a surprise outlook downgrade by ratings agency Fitch, and a tumbling stock market which has underperformed its European peers.
This has compounded a sense of crisis after hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in October and November to protest underfunding in education, the cost of living and the state of public services and housing.
The latest PMI survey has meanwhile raised the odds of France entering a technical recession — two consecutive prints of negative GDP growth — in the fourth quarter, according to Joe Hayes, senior principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The next print will follow a 0.1% contraction in the third quarter, though a revised Q3 reading is due on Friday.
"The eurozone's second-largest economy is struggling with weak domestic demand, in part due to hesitancy from clients to commit to projects ahead of a highly uncertain election period next year," Hayes said.
"We've subsequently seen a rapid deterioration in business confidence these past few months as other long-standing issues, such as concerns about France's fiscal position, resurface as the election draws closer."
"It's also notable that output price inflation has slowed sharply in November. This suggests that company pricing power has diminished and further highlights the fragility of the French economy," Hayes added.

Nvidia is paid by cloud companies such as Google. The clouds are paid by companies such as Nike and P&G. Those companies are paid by you at the checkout. So the last question in the chain is the simplest one. Can the shopper keep paying?

Is The Shopper Overextended?
On savings, yes. On debt, no.
We compared today’s shopper with two moments worth remembering. One is mid-2007, just before the housing bust. The other is the end of 2019, before the pandemic. The savings rate, 3.8%, is close to mid-2007’s 2.7%. The debt picture looks more like 2019.
Source: Trefis, using FRED data. Savings rate: September 2026. Debt payments and late card payments: second quarter of 2026. Household debt: first quarter of 2026.
So this is not 2007. Households owe far less compared with their income. Late payments on credit cards are near normal. What is thin is the cushion of savings.
Revolving credit, mostly credit-card balances, did reach a record $1.37 trillion. It is up 4.2% in a year. That is slower than spending, which rose 6.3% before inflation. And people feel the strain. Consumer sentiment, a survey of how people feel about their money and the economy, was 48 in October. That is near its record low of 44.8, set in May.
How Long Can It Last?
About a year, before savings fall below 2007’s level.
Spending is growing 1.5 percentage points faster than income. Another year like this would take the savings rate from 3.8% to about 2.3%. That is below mid-2007’s 2.7%. After that, shoppers would either borrow more or spend less. Their light debts would allow them to borrow more.
If they spend less, P&G, Pepsi and Nike would feel it first. Then, one link at a time, it would reach their cloud bills, Google’s capital spending and Nvidia’s sales.
Two things will decide it. One is whether income grows faster if inflation cools. The other is whether the Fed cuts the cost of the borrowing that shoppers can still afford.
The line to remember: the American shopper is paying P&G out of savings, not debt. That is safer than in 2007. But at this pace, savings fall below 2007’s level in about a year.

The question for shareholders is what SpaceX’s AI business really is. If its best AI money comes from leasing chips to rivals, the market may value that unit like a cloud landlord instead of a model builder.
Musk’s Metric Favors Renting Over Building
Musk reportedly told staff: “At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks. If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company. Move the needle on revenue.”
A GPU, the specialized chip that trains and runs AI models, earns cash every month when rented, while one spent training a model that trails rivals may earn nothing, so by his own measure renting wins until Grok closes the gap. An appeals court has struck down a federal law that requires workplaces to provide accommodations for pregnant women, saying Congress violated the U.S. Constitution when it passed the law in 2022.
The New Orleans-based 5th Circuit Court of Appeals issued its 9-8 decision on Friday. Advocates of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act said the decision invalidates the law in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, which are covered by the 5th Circuit, and could imperil the law elsewhere.
The appeals court said the act was unconstitutional because a majority of U.S. House members weren’t physically present when it was approved as part of a spending package in December 2022. At the time, the House was operating under COVID-era rules that allowed members to vote by proxy.
“The (Quorum) Clause’s text, context, original understanding and unbroken historical application all indicate that members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes — as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago and as Congress has done ever since the founding,” the court said in its decision. “‘Proxy presence’ does not count.”
A Better Balance, an advocacy group that spearheaded the law’s passage, said in a statement Friday that the circuit court ruling would likely be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Inimai Chettiar, the group’s president, said the ruling was “legally unsound and short-sighted.”
“The 5th Circuit has put the health, livelihoods, and economic security of millions of American women and their families at risk,” Chettiar said in a statement.
The law, which passed with bipartisan support, strengthens the rights of women to receive workplace accommodations for needs related to pregnancy and childbirth, such as time off for medical appointments and exemptions from heavy lifting.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued to block the act in 2023 on grounds that it was unconstitutional. In 2024, a federal judge agreed and blocked enforcement of the law for Texas state employees.
But in 2025, a three-judge panel on the 5th Circuit court disagreed, finding that the law was properly passed under Congress’s pandemic-era rules. That decision was appealed to the full 5th Circuit.
In their dissent, the eight judges who would have upheld the law noted that no member of Congress objected that a quorum was lacking when the $1.7 trillion government funding bill was passed.
“The State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause,” they wrote.
While the law was passed during the Biden administration, the Department of Justice under the Trump administration has continued to fight Paxton’s lawsuit, which — if successful — could open the door to legal challenges of other pandemic-era laws passed by proxy.
A message seeking comment on the appeals court decision was left Sunday with the Justice Department.

Many shoppers look forward to Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of scoring a good deal or two. Adobe forecasts that consumers will spend over $15 billion online on Cyber Monday and $12.9 billion on Black Friday, making them two of the biggest shopping days of the year.
However, for some shoppers, these holidays can cost them more than they bargained for. A separate study from McAfee found a 91% year-over-year spike in the number of Americans reporting holiday shopping scams, and 60% of those who lost money lost at least $100.
"Black Friday and Cyber Monday create a perfect environment for scammers because consumers are actively looking for deals and often make quick purchasing decisions," said Michael Bruemmer, vice president of global data breach resolution and consumer protection at Experian.

3 common holiday shopping scams and how to avoid them
Holiday shopping scams can take on many forms and be easy to miss. Shoppers rushing to get their holiday shopping done at the lowest possible prices may be less likely to notice a scam or vet purchases as carefully as they normally would.
Some of the most common holiday shopping scams include:
Phishing emails and text messages
Shoppers may receive fake text messages or emails from scammers posing as retailers or shipping companies.
"Phishing emails and text messages will always be a popular tactic for fraudsters, and the messages may appear to come from well-known retailers, shipping companies, or payment providers and are often designed to steal login credentials or financial information," said Bruemmer.
Legitimate retailers and shipping companies will never ask shoppers to share personal information via email or text. If you receive a text message or email that you suspect could be a phishing scheme, you can report this scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Gift card scams
Gift card scams occur year-round, but they tend to ramp up during the holiday season. Scammers may try to sell gift cards online at a "discount" and never send them, or sell cards whose balances have already been drained. Some scammers may even photograph gift cards in stores and wait for someone to purchase and load the card, then drain the balance.
When making any gift card purchases this holiday season, only purchase cards from trusted retailers or directly on the retailer's website rather than via a third-party website.
Fake online stores
Scammers may build fake websites that imitate trusted retailers to trick consumers into sharing their personal information. These websites can look quite convincing, but there are a few red flags to watch for that can help shoppers determine whether a website is legitimate.
This includes mobile apps or websites that ask shoppers to grant access to your contacts, text messages, stored passwords, or payment information. Other signs, such as misspelled words on the website or in the URL, discounts that are too good to be true, and limited or missing contact information, can also indicate that a website is fraudulent.
Shoppers can rely on tools such as Scamwise, ScamAdviser, and Google Safe Browsing to check whether a website is suspicious and receive alerts before visiting a fraudulent site.

Options command premiums because buyers are willing to pay for protection against adverse price movements or exposure to potentially favorable ones. The greater the expected volatility of the underlying asset, the more valuable those options generally become. Sellers collect those premiums upfront while accepting the obligation to absorb certain market outcomes.
But conventional options aren’t the only way to monetize volatility. Structured products can accomplish something similar, and one particularly popular category among financial advisors is the autocallable note. An autocallable is a structured debt instrument whose returns depend on the performance of an underlying asset, such as the Nasdaq-100 Index.
It typically offers a relatively high contingent coupon, but that income comes with conditions. If the underlying index falls below a predetermined barrier on an observation date, the coupon may be skipped. If the index performs well enough, the note can be automatically redeemed early. And if the index suffers a sufficiently large decline by maturity, investors can lose principal.
Traditionally, these products have been purchased individually through banks or advisors. But investors who want liquidity and diversification across multiple autocallables can now access the strategy through ETFs. Question for you, dear reader: While watching MLB games in 2026, did you at some point say to yourself, "Wow, the young talent in the game seems to be better than ever"?
If it seemed that way, that's because it was, at least among position players.
Position players aged 25 and under combined for 188.9 FanGraphs WAR this past season. That's the most in a single season in Major League history and more than five wins better than the previous high (2018, 183.8 fWAR).
So let's go around the diamond and highlight -- somewhat subjectively -- the best young player at each position.
Note: Players are presented with their 2027 season age.
Catcher: Carter Jensen, Royals (23)
When you pass Mike Piazza in the rookie catcher record books, you know you're doing something good. The 1993 National League Rookie of the Year and Hall of Famer held the record for most extra-base hits by a rookie backstop since at least 1947 -- until Jensen came along and recorded 64 XBHs this year. His 27 homers were a record for any Royals rookie.
Jensen, who was the AL Player of the Month in September, also improved behind the plate and will continue to learn from a Royals legend in 2027.
First base: Nick Kurtz, A's (24)
The unanimous American League Rookie of the Year in 2025, Kurtz was on his way to a stellar sophomore season before a right thumb strain essentially ended his year in early August. He finished with 21 homers and a 138 wRC+ in 99 games. Kurtz also had a robust 18.0% barrel rate. Kurtz's 152 wRC+ and 18.3% barrel rate since the start of 2025 are both tied for fourth among all players with at least 500 plate appearances.
Second base: JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals (24)
The Cardinals made Wetherholt their leadoff hitter for his MLB debut on Opening Day, and he immediately rewarded their belief in him. His offensive totals were fine in the end (17 homers, 101 wRC+ through 139 games), but the expected stats say Wetherholt was a little unlucky at the plate this season, and there are reasons to believe he can put up better numbers going forward.
Defensively, you couldn't ask for anything better. Wetherholt trailed only one player in MLB -- the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong -- in outs above average and fielding run value.
Third base: Kevin McGonigle, Tigers (22)
McGonigle was a first-round Draft pick out of high school just three years ago and was MLB Pipeline's No. 2 overall prospect heading into the 2026 season. But he didn't let the burden of high expectations weigh him down. Instead, McGonigle ran away with the AL Rookie of the Year Award.
Already possessing top-notch plate discipline, McGonigle produced a .376 on-base percentage (12th-best in MLB), 95 walks and 97 runs scored. He was the fourth rookie with 95 walks and 95 runs scored since the ROY Award was established in 1947, joining Aaron Judge (2017), Joe Morgan (1965) and Jim Gilliam (1953). His 5.4 fWAR tied for ninth-best in the sport.
Shortstop: Elly De La Cruz, Reds (25)
De La Cruz has been making mouths drop across the league for so long that it's hard to believe he won't turn 25 years old for another six weeks. His fourth season in the Majors was his best one yet: A .283/.365/.515 slash line, 30 homers, an 11.3% walk rate and a 139 wRC+ were just a few of the career-highs from Cincinnati's sensational shortstop. He finished fourth in the NL MVP voting. He also stole at least 30 bases for the fourth straight year, becoming only the fourth Reds player to accomplish a 30-30 season.

What started as a plan to detonate nearly 5 tons of degraded explosive material in Iowa, with coordination between the U.S. Army and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, has since triggered multiple state emergency responses and an “unprecedented” coordination of federal agencies.
The detonation is scheduled for Wednesday about 9 a.m. at the U.S. Army’s ammunition plant in Middletown in southeast Iowa. The scheduled time follows numerous delays over the past week from the Army, a lawsuit, intervention from the president, and widespread public concern of the health and environmental effects associated with detonating a lead-based explosive.
Lead deposition maps released by the Army Tuesday morning show lead released by the detonation could be dispersed in the air as far as 100 miles southwest of Middletown and cross into Missouri. An additional map shows there is a potential for lead surface dust to settle as far as 50 miles southwest of the detonation site.
The Army has recommended, and FEMA is supporting, the evacuation of Iowans in Middletown and the immediate area – a 5-mile cone to the southwest of the detonation site – during the detonation period.
Soldiers, environmental teams and other federal officials are in the area helping to sample soils and alert residents of the detonation plans. The Army will be releasing maps, adjusted for the latest weather conditions, six hours ahead of detonation and every hour leading up to detonation.
A slew of federal officials from the Army, the EPA, Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, Department of Agriculture and more gathered at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant Tuesday for a press conference and shared new information with the public about the response.
Relocation assistance
When the detonation was originally announced, the Army recommended individuals in a select neighborhood of Middletown evacuate during the detonation, due to concerns that the blast could cause some windows to shatter.
After nearly a week of nationwide, public outcry and calls from politicians for greater protections of the surrounding area, additional efforts are in place to mitigate the amount of lead dust that is emitted, and the government is working to help Iowans in the area.
